A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Dynamic Typography framework, with corresponding methods, experiments, figures and tables despite the revised title. All supplied pages are readable. v1 ends with references; v3 additionally contains Appendices A–G, which are included in this comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original animation experiments on 33 samples, quantitative baseline comparisons and component ablations in Tables 1–2, and qualitative comparisons across video backbones.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds a user preference study, control-point sensitivity results, font and language demonstrations, failure cases and GPT-4V-assisted examples.

M1.justification: Appendix G adds an optional GPT-4V procedure for selecting shape-compatible words, letters and prompts before animation. The core base-field/motion-field algorithm, SDS guidance, regularizers and frequency annealing remain. Newly disclosed optimization details do not establish that the earlier implementation changed.

E1.justification: The main 33-sample alphabet dataset is retained. Appendix D adds Chinese and Japanese character examples and tests with Segoe Print and Roboto-Bold alongside KaushanScript-Regular (Figures 13–15). These provide limited qualitative extensions of the existing task to additional scripts and font conditions.

E2.justification: Gen-2, DynamiCrafter and LiveSketch remain the comparison methods in Table 1 and Figure 8. The added user study uses the same comparator set. Word-as-Image remains an input-generation component, while GPT-4V is evaluated as a design assistant rather than a competing animation baseline.

E3.justification: Appendix E introduces a four-way human preference evaluation, with eight randomly sampled questions per user and 62 reported responses, considering legibility, semantic alignment and temporal consistency. New controlled experiments vary control-point counts between 75, 204 and 420 and compare regularization strengths. The newly stated frame count and rendering resolution document the retained comparison; they do not establish a changed protocol or rerun.

E4.justification: v3 substantially expands analysis through control-point sensitivity, same-letter font and prompt variations, an explicit legibility-versus-semantic-deformation failure case, and GPT-4V-assisted design examples. The frequency-encoding ablation moves to Appendix B and gains a butterfly example, but its quantitative Table 2 row is removed. The other component ablations and backbone comparison remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new user-study sample count and preference percentages add evaluation information and results, without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the retained Table 2 rows have identical scores. New Figure 16 reports preferences of 44.76% for Ours, 21.57% for LiveSketch, 19.96% for DynamiCrafter and 13.71% for Gen-2, alongside substantial new qualitative findings. v1's No Freq. results—0.02222 warping error, 0.5377 PIC and 20.8280 alignment—disappear. Consequently, the full model becomes the highest-PIC remaining ablation without any score improvement.

T1.justification: The written structure-loss definition in Equation 8 changes from an unweighted sum to separately weighted base-to-letter and inter-frame terms; Appendix A supplies unequal weights. This is a limited formal revision. The SDS and frequency-annealing mathematics are retained, and neither version adds theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains prompt-driven, legible vector animation through jointly optimized base and motion fields. v3's conclusion explicitly extends its generalizability claim to different fonts, prompts and languages, whereas v1 emphasizes arbitrary words, motion patterns and video backbones.

C2.justification: v3 explains that excessive control points promote self-intersections and that strong legibility regularization applied too early can suppress semantic deformation. Its rocket failure case makes the existing legibility–semantic-alignment limitation concrete, and Appendix G proposes shape-compatible input selection as mitigation. The underlying backbone and shape-mismatch limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly specifies Adam, separate learning rates, affine-motion scales, regularization weights, interleaved updates and gradual legibility weighting. Sections 3.1 and 5.1 add subdivision and rendering details. These substantially improve implementation disclosure without establishing changed experimental execution. Conversely, v1's explicit gradient-detachment instruction is omitted. The backbone, optimization budget, hardware/runtime and project link are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds references including VBench, HyperNeRF, D-NeRF, Creating Emordle and GPT-4, and removes the SVG specification reference. These support additional context and experiments; the central positioning against static typography, existing kinetic typography and LiveSketch remains.

P1.justification: v3 retitles the paper, substantially condenses and rewrites Related Work, reorganizes the method requirements, and edits explanations throughout. Frequency encoding and its ablation discussion move from the main text to Appendix B, while implementation material is organized in Appendix A. These constitute substantial editorial restructuring beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v3 changes the document typography, author block and layout, revises the framework diagram, restructures Figure 9 and Table 2, and changes score highlighting. Figures 11–18 add or reorganize ablation imagery, sensitivity comparisons, font/script examples, the user-study pie chart, failure cases and GPT-4V-assisted outputs. Some earlier imagery is reused rather than newly generated.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens reproducibility through missing optimizer and regularization details, and complements v1's automated metrics with direct human preference evidence. New sensitivity and failure analyses also make applicability easier to assess. These gains outweigh the removed numerical frequency ablation and omitted gradient-detachment instruction, although the user study still lacks uncertainty reporting. The improvement comes from stronger documentation and validation, not higher main comparison scores.
